title: The Relative Benefits of Green Versus Lean Office Space: Three Field Experiments
research_question: To examine the impact of lean and 'green' offices on subjective perceptions of air quality, concentration, and workplace satisfaction as well as objective measures of productivity, and to investigate the long-term effects and underlying mechanisms.

participants.description: Study 1: N=67 (final sample), 39 men, 28 women, age 23-53 (M=30.02), consultants in London, UK. Study 2: N=81 (final sample), 15 men, 66 women, age 21-59 (M=34.86), health insurance call center agents in Zwolle, The Netherlands. Study 3: N=33, 16 men, 17 women, age 22-33 (M=28.0), consultancy organization employees in London, UK.
participants.recruitment: Email invitations (Study 1), paper-and-pencil questionnaires via manager (Study 2), voluntary and unpaid (Study 3).

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Lean office: minimalist, stripped of extraneous decorations, no plants. Green office: lean office enriched with living, large-leafed plants (average height 90 cm). Study 1: 3 plants per 5 desks. Study 2: 1 plant per 3 desks. Study 3: 8 large plants in the space, at least 3 visible from workstation.

mechanisms: Plants restore directed attention capacity (Attention Restoration Theory).
Enrichment signals managerial care and attention, leading to increased work engagement and reduced disengagement.
Reduced disengagement leads to increased workplace satisfaction, concentration, and perceived air quality.
implementation_implications: Introducing plants into a previously lean office significantly increases workplace satisfaction, self-reported levels of concentration, perceived air quality, and actual productivity.
These improvements are sustained over the short-term and long-term.
Green working environments are more enjoyable, conducive to concentration, and more productive for businesses than lean equivalents.
Office landscaping strategies that involve transforming a lean office into a green one contribute to employee welfare and organizational output.

limitations: Study 1: Workplace satisfaction increased in both lean and green conditions, possibly due to visual exposure to plants in the lean condition as participants walked past them.
Study 2: Concentration effects did not reach statistical significance, although a small increase was observed in the green condition.
Call-center productivity (AHT) in Study 2 was an ambiguous measure, potentially valuing speed over quality, making interpretation difficult.
The focus was on a narrow band of potential environmental options (lean vs. green).
Study 3 had a small sample size, requiring replication across tasks and contexts.
The research did not include a measure of creativity.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Exposure to natural environments can restore directed attention and reduce mental fatigue, leading to improved cognitive performance.
Humans have an innate tendency to connect with nature, and this connection promotes psychological well-being and performance.

mechanism_chain.description: The presence of plants in the office environment is hypothesized to improve well-being and productivity by enhancing perceived air quality, reducing stress, and restoring cognitive resources.
